text.p: Former top soldier Ehud Barak is the first new face at the helm of Israel's Labour party in 20 years and could blunt the security edge Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu enjoyed at the polls.

Barak, 55, hopes 35 years of military service, a record as Israel's most decorated soldier and his role in dramatic undercover operations will make him an attractive alternative to the right-wing Netanyahu in a country obsessed with security.
Elections are scheduled in three years.

A year ago Netanyahu, the 47-year-old right-wing Likud leader and former commando, defeated prime minister Shimon Peres of Labour by promising to deliver peace with security following a wave of suicide bombings.

"I'm convinced I have the power to defeat Netanyahu and to return us to control of the country," Barak wrote in an election leaflet before sweeping to victory in Tuesday's Labour ballot for party leader.
A Gallup opinion poll of 491 Israeli Jews last month showed Barak neck and neck with Netanyahu who is grappling with a peace process in crisis and a still lingering corruption scandal.

Like his assassinated mentor Yitzhak Rabin, Barak has a blunt demeanour popular with Israelis. He left the army barely two years ago and joined Rabin's government as interior minister. He served as foreign minister under Peres, 73.
Barak's election marks a milestone for Labour. The rival camps of Peres and Rabin had ruled the party for 23 years.

His image contrasts sharply with that of Peres, regarded by many Israelis as too soft on security. Even Rabin's widow Leah has called Barak heir to the legacy of her late husband, who was army chief in the 1967 Six-Day War.

Barak, who once commanded Netanyahu in an elite unit, made a name for himself in 1973 when, as a commando posing as a woman, he took part in a foray into Beirut during which three PLO leaders were killed.
Speaking about himself in the third-person in a television interview two years ago, Barak said: "He has been in the field 35 years and personally led dozens of operations.
"He has been shot at, not just once, from a distance no further than that between you and me. He has shot people from a distance at which you see the white of their eyes," the former general said.

Military sources said Barak devised many of the tactics used to combat the Palestinian uprising. On the eve of his leaving the army, Barak took pride in the deaths of 10 of 12 most-wanted guerrillas and vowed his forces would hunt the others down.

Foreign sources have said that in a bid to snuff out the revolt in its early days Barak planned and commanded the 1988 raid in Tunis during which PLO military commander Khalil al-Wazir, better known as Abu Jihad, was killed.

But he opposed trying to crush the revolt with unrestrained force and warned rampaging Jewish settlers against taking the law into their own hands. As a member of Labour, Barak favours swapping land for peace with both Palestinians and Syria.

While army chief, Barak oversaw the first handovers of occupied land to Palestinians under peace deals with the PLO. He helped clinch peace with Jordan in 1994. He met his Syrian counterpart for unproductive security talks in Washington.
His army career is not without blemishes.

He has battled allegations he abandoned wounded soldiers in a training accident while chief of staff in 1992. He says they were already on evacuation helicopters under expert medical care when he left the scene.

In 1991 he sparked a row by going public with news of undercover soldiers posing as Arabs. The army said the disclosure aimed to deter Palestinian hostilities. Barak's critics accused him of having political motivations.

Born on a kibbutz collective settlement, Barak studied physics and mathematics at Jerusalem's Hebrew University and earned a master's degree in economic engineering systems from Stanford University in California.
